title: Four thousand years of secrets
dek: From an Egyptian scribe's odd hieroglyphs to the post-quantum standards of 2024: the ciphers, the breaks and the people. Filter by chapter to follow one thread.

eras.label: c. 1900 BC – AD 799
eras.title: Antiquity
eras.text: Unusual signs, transposition with a staff, and the shift that carries Caesar's name.

eras.title: Baghdad and the Renaissance
eras.text: Arab scholars invent cryptanalysis; Italian courts answer with many alphabets.

eras.title: Black chambers and indecipherable ciphers
eras.text: Every European court reads its neighbours' mail; Vigenère resists for three centuries.

eras.title: Machines and world wars
eras.text: Radio makes every message public; rotor machines and the people who broke them decide battles.

eras.title: Information theory and the computer
eras.text: Shannon turns secrecy into mathematics; IBM brings cryptography to banks; DES is born.

eras.title: The public-key revolution
eras.text: Keys that can be published, signatures, and the first battles over who may use strong cryptography.

eras.label: 2001 – today
eras.title: Cryptography everywhere
eras.text: Open competitions, broken hashes, encrypted-by-default Internet, and the race against quantum computers.

events.label: c. 1900 BC
events.title: Unusual hieroglyphs at Menet Khufu
events.text: A tomb inscription replaces standard hieroglyphs with rare ones, the oldest known deliberate transformation of writing.

events.label: c. 1500 BC
events.title: A secret glaze recipe
events.text: A clay tablet hides a recipe for pottery glaze by writing words with uncommon cuneiform signs: a trade secret, encrypted.

events.label: c. 500 BC
events.title: The scytale
events.text: A strip of leather wound around a staff: a transposition cipher whose key is the staff's thickness.

events.label: c. 50 BC
events.title: Caesar's cipher
events.text: Suetonius records that Caesar replaced each letter by the one three places further on.

events.label: c. 850
events.title: Frequency analysis
events.text: In Baghdad, the first written description of cryptanalysis by counting letters. Rediscovered in an Istanbul archive in 1987.

events.title: The cipher disk
events.text: Two concentric alphabets that can turn: the first polyalphabetic cipher, and the ancestor of every rotor machine.

events.title: The keyword cipher
events.text: A repeating keyword chooses the shift of each letter. History will credit it to Blaise de Vigenère.

events.title: Mary Stuart is executed
events.text: Walsingham's cryptanalyst reads Mary's letters to the Babington plotters; the decrypts are the evidence at her trial.

events.title: Playfair, and Vigenère broken
events.text: Wheatstone invents the digraph cipher named after Lord Playfair; Babbage breaks Vigenère but does not publish.

events.title: Kasiski's examination
events.text: Distances between repeated fragments reveal the length of a Vigenère key. The indecipherable cipher falls in public.

events.title: The first one-time pad
events.text: A Californian banker publishes a telegraph code with random additives used once. Forgotten until 2011.

events.title: Kerckhoffs's principle
events.text: “La cryptographie militaire”: a cipher must stay secure even if the enemy knows everything about it except the key.

events.title: The Zimmermann telegram
events.text: British codebreakers read a German offer of alliance to Mexico; its publication helps bring the United States into the First World War.

events.title: Vernam's teleprinter cipher
events.text: Key tape combined bit by bit with the message. Used once and truly random, it becomes the one-time pad.

events.title: Enigma is patented
events.text: A rotor machine for businesses; the German navy adopts it in 1926 and the army in 1928.

events.title: The index of coincidence
events.text: Statistics replaces guesswork: the probability that two letters agree measures how polyalphabetic a ciphertext is.

events.title: Rejewski breaks Enigma
events.text: Permutation theory and the doubled message key let the Polish Cipher Bureau reconstruct the rotors and read German traffic.

events.title: The Pyry meeting
events.text: Five weeks before the invasion, the Poles give their British and French allies their methods and two Enigma replicas.

events.title: The bombe
events.text: At Bletchley Park, electromechanical machines test rotor settings against cribs. Ultra intelligence follows.

events.title: Venona begins
events.text: Soviet one-time pads printed twice let American analysts read thousands of messages and expose atomic spies.

events.title: Colossus
events.text: The first programmable electronic digital computer attacks the Lorenz cipher of the German high command.

events.title: Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems
events.text: Perfect secrecy, unicity distance, confusion and diffusion: cryptography becomes a branch of mathematics.

events.title: Non-secret encryption
events.text: At GCHQ, Ellis shows that public-key encryption is possible in principle. Kept secret until 1997.

events.title: Lucifer and the Feistel network
events.text: IBM's cipher for banks, built from rounds that need not be invertible. Clifford Cocks finds RSA at GCHQ the same year, in secret.

events.title: DES
events.text: The first public encryption standard: 64-bit blocks, a 56-bit key and S-boxes hardened against an attack nobody else knew.

events.title: New Directions in Cryptography
events.text: Two strangers agree on a secret in public. Ralph Merkle's puzzles had shown the way.

events.title: RSA
events.who: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman
events.text: A public-key cipher and signature scheme based on the difficulty of factoring. Martin Gardner's column challenges readers to break RSA-129.

events.title: Password hashing with salt
events.text: Unix stores salted, iterated DES-based hashes of passwords, never the passwords themselves.

events.title: Merkle–Damgård
events.text: Iterating a compression function: the construction of MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2 (proved secure by Damgård in 1989).

events.title: Elliptic-curve cryptography
events.text: The same protocols in the group of points of a curve, with much shorter keys.

events.title: Differential cryptanalysis
events.text: Following differences through the rounds breaks many ciphers, but not DES, whose designers had known it since 1974.

events.title: PGP
events.text: Pretty Good Privacy brings RSA to everyone's e-mail; the US government investigates its author for exporting munitions.

events.title: MD5
events.text: A 128-bit hash that becomes ubiquitous. Collisions are found in 2004.

events.title: Blowfish and linear cryptanalysis
events.text: A free alternative to DES, and a new attack that breaks DES with 2⁴³ known plaintexts.

events.title: Shor's algorithm
events.text: A quantum computer could factor and compute discrete logarithms in polynomial time, breaking RSA and elliptic curves.

events.title: HMAC
events.who: Mihir Bellare, Ran Canetti, Hugo Krawczyk
events.text: A keyed hash with a security proof, immune to length extension. Lov Grover finds quantum search the same year.

events.title: Deep Crack
events.text: A \$250,000 machine finds a DES key in 56 hours: the 56-bit key is officially too short.

events.title: bcrypt
events.text: Blowfish's slow key setup, repeated 2^cost times, becomes OpenBSD's password hash.

events.title: AES
events.text: Rijndael wins NIST's open competition and becomes the Advanced Encryption Standard, FIPS 197.

events.title: Padding oracles
events.text: A server that reveals whether padding is valid lets an attacker decrypt CBC ciphertexts byte by byte.

events.title: MD5 collisions; GCM
events.who: Xiaoyun Wang; David McGrew, John Viega
events.text: Wang's team finds collisions in MD5 in hours. The same year, Galois/Counter Mode is proposed.

events.title: Learning with errors
events.text: A noisy linear-algebra problem as hard as worst-case lattice problems: the basis of ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

events.title: Curve25519
events.text: A curve designed so that the simple, fast implementation is also the safe one. Its key exchange, X25519, becomes the Internet's default.

events.title: ChaCha
events.text: An add-rotate-xor stream cipher, fast and constant-time in software; with Poly1305 it becomes a standard AEAD.

events.title: scrypt
events.text: The first widely used memory-hard password hash. RockYou leaks 32 million plaintext passwords the same year.

events.title: Sony's ECDSA nonce
events.text: The PlayStation 3 signs with the same nonce every time, which reveals Sony's private key.

events.title: Ed25519
events.text: Deterministic, fast elliptic-curve signatures with no random nonce to get wrong.

events.title: Snowden and Dual_EC_DRBG
events.text: Leaked documents confirm an NSA back door in a standardised random number generator and push the web towards encryption by default.

events.title: SHA-3 and Argon2
events.text: The sponge construction becomes FIPS 202; Argon2 wins the Password Hashing Competition.

events.title: NIST's post-quantum competition
events.text: 82 candidates for replacing RSA and elliptic curves enter eight years of public attack.

events.title: SHAttered
events.text: Two different PDF files with the same SHA-1, after 9 quintillion SHA-1 computations.

events.title: TLS 1.3
events.text: Only authenticated encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) and forward-secret key exchange remain.

events.title: SIKE broken
events.text: An isogeny-based finalist falls in an hour on a laptop. NIST selects Kyber and Dilithium.

events.title: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA
events.text: FIPS 203, 204 and 205: the first post-quantum standards. Browsers, Signal and iMessage already use hybrid key exchange.

events.title: Post-quantum by default
events.text: OpenSSH 10 makes ML-KEM hybrid key exchange its default; a large share of web traffic is already post-quantum.
